title: From Despair to Unexpected Mercy
overview: The prophet grieves a society where no one can be trusted, then turns to hope that God will forgive his people, restore them and keep his old promises.

parts.label: A harvest with nothing left (vv. 1-4)
parts.note: Micah compares looking for an honest person to searching a picked-over vineyard and finding no fruit at all. Rulers, judges and the wealthy work together to twist justice for bribes, so even the best of them are like thorn bushes that hurt anyone who comes near.

parts.label: No one to trust (vv. 5-6)
parts.note: The breakdown reaches into homes: friends, spouses and children turn on each other. Jesus later echoed verse 6 when he warned that following him could divide families.

parts.label: Waiting in the dark (vv. 7-10)
parts.note: Speaking for the whole people, the prophet admits they have sinned and will bear the consequences, yet trusts God to bring them back into the light. The enemy who mocks "Where is your God?" is spoken of as a woman, probably a rival nation or city, though scholars are unsure which one.

parts.label: Walls rebuilt, people return (vv. 11-13)
parts.note: A day is promised when the ruined city's walls are rebuilt and people stream in from Assyria, Egypt and every distant place. The Hebrew of verse 11 is unclear, and verse 13 may mean the wider world or Israel's own land must first face the results of its wrongdoing.

parts.label: Shepherd us again (vv. 14-17)
parts.note: The prophet asks God to care for his people like a shepherd and let them graze again in Bashan and Gilead, rich pastures east of the Jordan River that Israel had lost. God answers with a promise of wonders like the escape from Egypt, and the nations that once boasted are left speechless and humbled, as low as a snake in the dust.

parts.label: Who is a God like you? (vv. 18-20)
parts.note: The book closes by praising a God who does not stay angry forever but enjoys showing mercy, pictured as throwing sins into the deep sea. The opening question plays on Micah's own name, which means "Who is like the LORD?", and the final lines recall God's ancient promises to Abraham and Jacob.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether the promised restoration was fulfilled in the Jewish return from exile in Babylon, is fulfilled spiritually in the church, or still points to a future restoration of Israel.
think: When the people and institutions around you prove untrustworthy, what, if anything, keeps you from giving up hope?
